# CPU optimizations

@difference Extension: the runtime uses optional CPU instruction sets when the CPU has them, and allocates from its own allocator instead of the Windows heap; `BLITZLLVM_CPU` and a few `BLITZLLVM_*` variables control and debug both.

Neither changes the result of a program.

## CPU features

Programs are compiled for the generic target of their architecture (x86-64 with SSE2, or ARMv8.0 with NEON on arm64). The runtime asks the CPU once which optional instruction sets exist, and code that is faster with one only runs when the CPU has it. Today that is `LockBuffer` and `UnlockBuffer` swapping the red and blue channels of 32 bit buffers (SSSE3 and AVX2 on x86-64, NEON on arm64). Every faster version gives the same bytes as the plain one, and floats are never fused into multiply-adds there.

`BLITZLLVM_CPU` lowers what the runtime may use, which is how each code path is tested without owning every CPU. It never adds a feature the CPU lacks. It holds a comma separated list:

| Setting | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| `baseline` | No optional features: SSE2 only on x86-64, NEON only on arm64. |
| `v2`, `v3`, `v4` | x86-64 only: at most the features of the x86-64-v2, -v3 or -v4 level (v4 is AVX-512). |
| `native` | What the CPU has. This is the default. |
| `-<feature>` | Removes a feature and everything that needs it, such as `-avx2`, `-fma`, `-sse4.1`, `-dotprod` or `-sve2`. |

For example `BLITZLLVM_CPU=v3,-fma` runs as an AVX2 machine without FMA. A program started with `--profile` and `BLITZ_FPS=1` prints the result as `cpu: x86_64 v3: sse3 ssse3 ...` before the first frame report.

## Memory allocator

Strings, objects, arrays, banks and the runtime itself ask for memory very often, so BlitzLLVM answers most requests itself instead of calling the heap of the operating system each time. Small blocks (up to 32 KiB) are cut from large spans and kept in free lists per thread, so allocating and freeing take no lock and no system call. Larger blocks go to the system allocator. Spans that have been entirely free for more than a second are given back to the system, so a program that once needed a lot of small blocks (a level that was loaded and freed) does not keep that memory. Memory that is given back reads as zero when it is used again.

The allocator is used for `new` and `delete` of the runtime on every platform, and for `malloc`, `free` and the related C functions on Linux with glibc, so the libraries a program loads use it too (turn that off when building with `-DBLITZ_REPLACE_MALLOC=OFF`). On Windows and macOS the libraries (FFmpeg, the image and audio codecs, the Vulkan driver) keep using the system allocator, which is safe: `free` and `realloc` of a block from elsewhere are passed on.

To debug memory problems, set these before the program starts:

| Variable | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| `BLITZLLVM_DEBUG_ALLOC=1` | Freed blocks are filled with a pattern; a block written to after it was freed, or freed twice, stops the program with a message. New blocks are filled with another pattern so reading what was never written stands out. Blocks never freed are reported at the end (a few dozen kept by the C++ library are normal). Slower. |
| `BLITZLLVM_DEBUG_ALLOC_STATS=1` | Counts the blocks and bytes that were not freed and reports them at the end. |
| `BLITZLLVM_ALLOC_RELEASE=0` | Keeps spans instead of giving empty ones back, to compare memory use over time. |
| `BLITZLLVM_DEBUG_ALLOC_RELEASE=1` | Prints a line to stderr for every sweep that gave spans back. |
| `BLITZLLVM_ALLOC_SYSTEM=1` | Everything goes to the system allocator, for valgrind, AddressSanitizer and heap profilers. |
